answer: The notion evolved through several stages across 2008. April 21-28 (t0383): Martin Doerr opened the issue noting 'increasing claims of compatibility with the CIDOC CRM' and proposed a minimal working definition (ability to represent certain kinds of possibly multiple events associated with a Thing or Actor), which triggered a broad debate: Edmund Lee distinguished system compliance from dataset compliance; Nicholas Crofts laid out two compliance paradigms (independently verifiable criteria vs. certification authority), proposed graded conformance levels and a compatibility logo; Stephen Stead framed compatibility as 'no semantic loss' through data transforms and proposed concrete interoperability test questions; Guenther Goerz challenged whether strict compatibility can even be decided given the CRM's natural-language scope notes; Nick Poole (Collections Trust) offered to help build certification infrastructure. May 28 (t0392): after the May CRM-SIG meeting, Martin circulated 'an analysis of the requirement' distilled from the email debate, with a tentative plan to have a normative draft ready before the CIDOC 2008 conference for plenary approval. September 2-13 (t0400): Martin circulated a full draft text fleshing out the May decisions, introducing the core criterion of encoding 'without loss of meaning with respect to the CRM concepts' -- judged by an expert conversant in both source and CRM, not by an automatic test -- and allowing communities to restrict compatibility to an explicitly declared subset of CRM concepts. Vladimir Ivanov pushed on intensional/extensional meaning and asked for a counterexample of incompatibility; Martin supplied one ('Physical Object has date: Time-Span' as import/export-incompatible). October 7 (t0407): Martin sent a formal 'Call for Comment' on 'Definition of compatibility with ISO21127' (document V4, tied to CRM v4.2.6), meant to replace the old 'Compatibility with the CRM' section and to give high-level objectives/criteria (not a full logical definition), plus a minimal OWL 'reduced CRM-compatible form,' for discussion at the Nov 6-7 London SIG meeting. November 3 (t0417): Bernhard Schiemann sent a detailed section-by-section critique of V4; Martin's point-by-point replies pinned down the definition: a 'CRM-compatible form' is any encoding of CRM instances in a formal language that preserves the relations between CRM classes, properties and inheritance rules (explicitly excluding cardinality restrictions, which would violate the CRM's intended monotonic schema); a 'reduced CRM-compatible form' is a declared subset such that every instance of the reduced form is also a valid instance of the full CRM-compatible form; the draft distinguished import-compatible, export-compatible (and partial versions of each), and access-compatible (integrated-access) systems, with 'semantic reduction to CRM concepts' as the export mechanism. November 4-6 (t0420): a side vote settled the wording of the verification/certification clause, with members (Marco Neumann, Christian-Emil Ore, Bernhard Schiemann) debating options and converging on an alternative requiring providers to publish verification procedures or obtain third-party certification. November 14-16 (t0427): following the London meeting, Martin circulated CIDOC CRM v4.3 containing the adopted compatibility chapter, with a final vote on the closing certification phrase: 'The provider should be able to demonstrate the claim with suitable test data... The provider should either make evidence of these procedures publicly available on the Internet on a site nominated by the ISO community of use, so that any third party is able to verify the claim with suitable test data, or acquire a certificate by a certification authority (CA)... The CA will grant the provider of the certified system the right to use the "CRM compatible" logo.' Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore approved; this became part of CRM version 5.0, to be submitted to ISO as a proposed amendment to ISO 21127.
notes: Strong, dense coverage: seven threads spanning April through November 2008 trace the issue from Martin's initial open question through the May SIG analysis, the September draft, the October call for comment, the November London review/critique with Martin's clarifying replies (which pin down the actual definition), a side vote on the certification clause, and the final adoption vote producing CRM v4.3/5.0. No gaps found; the trail was continuous and each search led directly to the next relevant thread via thread ids and topic terms.
